title: Greeting and ordering
summary: Understand the waiter's first questions and order a drink and a bite politely, with quantities and preferences.
prereqText: None. You do not need any Spanish. Spanish spelling is close to its sound; accents mark stress and do not change how you read the letters.

blocks.html:
It is 9:30 in Madrid. You are standing at the bar of a busy café. A waiter looks at you, says something quickly, and waits. You want a coffee with milk and a slice of Spanish omelette. What do you say first, and what was the question?

In this lesson you will meet the five or six sentences that make up most of a café exchange, so that the waiter's speed becomes manageable.

Think of a café exchange as a short script with fixed slots: greeting, the waiter's "what will you have?", your order (item + please), a possible extra question, then thanks. You do not need to build sentences from scratch; you swap items into the same frame: un ___, por favor.
blocks.limits: Real waiters improvise, speak fast, and some skip parts of the script. The script is a starting scaffold for listening, not a guarantee of what you will hear.

blocks.purpose: Show the order of turns in a café exchange so the learner can predict what comes next.
blocks.alt: A flow of five boxes from left to right: greeting, the waiter asks what you want, you order an item with por favor, the waiter asks if you want anything else or for here or to go, you say thanks.

blocks.title: The frame and its parts
blocks.html:
Greeting. Hola works at any hour. Buenos días (morning), buenas tardes (afternoon), buenas noches (evening). Course decision: start with the time-of-day greeting; it sounds polite and costs nothing.

Ordering. The simplest polite frame is article + item, por favor: Un café con leche, por favor. Spanish nouns have gender: un café, un zumo, un bocadillo (masculine); una cerveza, una tostada, una tortilla (feminine). Use un/una for one, and a number plus plural for more: dos cafés, tres cervezas. Plural: add -s after a vowel, -es after a consonant (café → cafés only adds -s because the final é is a vowel).

Preferences. con = with, sin = without, solo = black (espresso, no milk), con leche = with milk, sin azúcar = without sugar, con hielo = with ice. Para tomar aquí = to have here, para llevar = to take away.

Other ways to order you will hear or may use: Quería un café, Me pones un café (to someone addressed as tú), Me pone un café (to someone addressed as usted), Póngame un café. Course decision: at A1, stick to Un ___, por favor and add quería as a second option. The others are for recognising.

What the waiter asks. ¿Qué le pongo? / ¿Qué te pongo? (What can I get you?), ¿Qué va a tomar? / ¿Qué quieres tomar? (What will you have?), ¿Algo más? (Anything else?), ¿Para tomar aquí o para llevar? (Here or to go?).

Status of these claims: the phrases are standard beginner Spanish. I could not verify them against the Plan curricular or RAE (sources unavailable when written); regional variation is real (for example caña for a small draught beer is common in Spain but not universal). Treat the list as a safe core, not a complete inventory.

blocks.title: Building one order, step by step

steps.prompt: Goal: two coffees with milk and one orange juice.
steps.html: Split the order into items: 2 × café con leche; 1 × zumo de naranja.
Choose quantities and agreement: dos cafés con leche (plural: add -s to the noun; con leche stays unchanged). One juice: un zumo de naranja (zumo is masculine).

steps.prompt: How do you join the two items and stay polite?
steps.html: Join with y (and) and finish with por favor: Dos cafés con leche y un zumo de naranja, por favor.
Handle different preferences by splitting the order into separate items rather than building a long sentence: Un café con leche y un café solo, por favor.

blocks.result: Frame: [quantity + item] + y + [quantity + item] + por favor. One word changes per slot.

blocks.prompt: A waiter says: "¿Qué le pongo?" What do you think he wants to know?
options: What you would like to order

feedback.0: He might ask that at a restaurant, but "poner" here is "to put/serve": he is asking what to serve you.
feedback.2: How are you is "¿Qué tal?" or "¿Cómo está?". Greetings come before the order.

blocks.explanation: ¿Qué le pongo? literally 'what do I put (down) for you?', a very common way for the waiter to ask for your order.

blocks.instructions: Read the dialogue (use the audio button if your browser offers it). First answer the comprehension questions without looking at the translations. Then type your own order in the production task.
blocks.debrief: You should have noticed the fixed frame: greeting, waiter's question, your order with por favor, a follow-up, thanks. The synthetic voice is useful for rhythm only; it is not a native speaker, so confirm pronunciation with your friend or real recordings.

lines.speaker: Camarero
lines.translation: Good morning. What can I get you?

lines.speaker: Tú
lines.text: Buenos días. Un café con leche y una tostada con tomate, por favor.
lines.translation: Good morning. A coffee with milk and a toast with tomato, please.

options: Coffee with milk and a toast with tomato
comprehension.explanation: 'Un café con leche y una tostada con tomate'.

feedback.0: Té and bocadillo are not in the dialogue.
feedback.2: Cerveza and tortilla do not appear here.

comprehension.prompt: What does "¿Para tomar aquí o para llevar?" ask?
options: Whether you will eat/drink here or take it away
comprehension.explanation: Aquí = here, llevar = to carry / take away.

feedback.2: Payment is covered in lesson 2 (tarjeta / efectivo).

production.prompt: Order a coffee with milk, politely.
accept: un café con leche, por favor
un café con leche por favor
quería un café con leche, por favor
póngame un café con leche, por favor
me pone un café con leche, por favor
production.accentHint: Check the accent on café and quería; the app is lenient on accents here.
production.tips: Frame: un + item + por favor. Accents on café remind you to stress the final syllable.
Number + plural noun. Cerveza is feminine; plural cervezas.
production.model: Dos cervezas, por favor. (Dos cañas also works in much of Spain: caña is a small draught beer.)

blocks.instructions: Fill each blank with the article, number or word that fits. Think about gender (un/una) and quantity before you type.
blocks.debrief: Masculine nouns take un, feminine take una; counting makes the noun plural. Con and sin express preferences.

config.hint: Masculine: café, zumo, bocadillo. Feminine: cerveza, tostada, tortilla.
config.text:
[[Un::masculine, 1]] café con leche, por favor.

[[Una::feminine, 1]] cerveza, por favor.

[[Dos::2]] zumos de naranja, por favor.

Un café [[sin::without]] azúcar, por favor.

Un té [[con::with]] limón, por favor.

blocks.task: Write (in Spanish, on paper or in the answer box on the Progress page notes) the order for: 3 coffees with milk and 1 water. Use the frame from the worked example.
hints: 3 = tres, 1 = una (botella de) agua or un agua.
Plural of café: cafés. Join with y. End with por favor.
rubric: Number and plural noun agree (tres cafés)
blocks.solution: Tres cafés con leche y un agua, por favor. (Agua is feminine but takes un/el in the singular because of the stressed initial a; this rule is from general Spanish grammar and was not re-verified here. Alternative that avoids it: una botella de agua.)

blocks.task: With your Spanish-speaking friend (voice, video or in person), role-play the exchange twice. You are the customer; your friend is the waiter and may improvise. Order one drink and one food item with one preference (for example sin azúcar or para llevar). Then swap, so you hear yourself as the waiter too.
rubric: Greeted with the right time-of-day greeting
Replied to a follow-up question (¿Algo más?)
blocks.externalFeedback: Ask your friend after the role-play: (1) Did I sound polite? (2) Which word was hard to understand? (3) One thing a real waiter would say differently. The app cannot judge pronunciation or tone; no microphone tools are used.
blocks.model: Buenos días. Un café solo y una tortilla, por favor. ¿Para tomar aquí? Sí, aquí. Gracias.

questions.prompt: The waiter asks "¿Algo más?" You want nothing else. The best reply is…

feedback.1: That says you DO want something (a coffee).
feedback.2: Por favor means please; it does not answer the question.

questions.explanation: Nada más = nothing more; gracias keeps it polite.

questions.prompt: Which order is correct for two beers?

feedback.0: After dos the noun must be plural: cervezas.
feedback.2: Un is singular and masculine; cerveza is feminine and you are ordering two.

questions.prompt: How do you say you want your coffee without sugar?
In your own words: how is a café order built in Spanish, and what two things must you check in each item?
rubric: Mentions gender (un/una) and plural for quantity
questions.model: Quantity or article + item, then por favor. Check the gender (un/una) and plural when you order more than one.

blocks.task: New situation: you are at a terrace with a friend in the afternoon. Write what you would say to order for both of you: one beer and one orange juice, and one portion of tortilla to share, to eat here. Then write what you would reply if the waiter asks "¿Algo más?".
rubric: Correct items with un/una and por favor
Mentions para tomar aquí or equivalent, or a clear order without it
blocks.model: Buenas tardes. Una cerveza, un zumo de naranja y una tortilla para compartir, por favor. Para tomar aquí. — Nada más, gracias.

blocks.prompt: Which part of the exchange would you find hardest to follow in a real café, and what could you do in your weekly practice to prepare for it?
